new_value: The Iroquois opened in 1912 at 413 South Rampart Street as a vaudeville and picture house, and it was among the first theaters anywhere to present jazz and blues as a show to sit and listen to. A house band accompanied silent films and touring acts such as headliner Butler "String Beans" May; pianist Clarence Williams and guitarist Lonnie Johnson performed here, and a young Louis Armstrong won a talent contest on its stage. Live shows ended about 1920 and the building carried on as a movie theater. Listed on the National Register of Historic Places, it still stands, vacant and closed to the public, on a block crowded with early jazz landmarks.

new_value: Two joined buildings at South Rampart and Perdido streets formed one of the first regular homes of jazz. The Odd Fellows and Masonic Hall was established in 1897, with a third-floor ballroom for dances; the Eagle Saloon opened next door in 1908 and became a gathering place for musicians. Buddy Bolden, John Robichaux, Frankie Dusen, Sidney Bechet, Bunk Johnson, King Oliver, Freddie Keppard and Baby Dodds are all tied to the site, and brass band parades set out from the door. The saloon building at 401 South Rampart survives, long vacant and closed to the public; its nonprofit owner fenced it and sought permits to clear the damaged interior in late 2025.

new_value: Sid Williams, a St. Martinville native, opened this dance hall at 1523 North St. Antoine Street in 1984. His younger brother Nathan Williams started Nathan and the Zydeco Cha-Chas by playing Friday nights here, and Buckwheat Zydeco was a frequent performer in the club's early years; Clifton Chenier and Rockin' Dopsie also played the room. From 1986 Williams ran a Thanksgiving food drive from the club. He died on February 2, 2025, aged 73, and his family described El Sid O's as one of the last zydeco clubs still standing in Louisiana. The club has kept his annual holiday food drive going, announcing another for November 2026.

new_value: The Jolly Inn on Barrow Street opened in 1998 and took its name from an older dance hall near Houma where founder Werlien Prosperie had gone with his parents as a boy and later played guitar and sang. Prosperie, who played accordion in a band called Couche Couche, built the new hall around live Cajun bands, and his daughter Sonia McNamara took it over. An earlier television report described dances on Friday nights and Sunday afternoons running through two-steps, waltzes, line dances and swamp pop; the current schedule could not be confirmed, so call before visiting. The family has said it may be the only dance hall left between New Orleans and Lafayette.
